question: An 18-year-old man comes to the physician because of severe left shoulder pain after a basketball match. During the game, the patient sustained an injury to the posterior part of his outstretched arm after being blocked by a defender. Examination shows no gross deformity of the left shoulder. Palpation of the shoulder elicits mild tenderness. Internal rotation of the arm against resistance shows weakness. These findings are most specific for injury to which of the following muscles?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Shoulder injury" -> "pain and tenderness" -> "internal rotation weakness" -> "subscapularis muscle involvement" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Shoulder injury" -> "pain and tenderness" -> "internal rotation weakness" -> "teres minor muscle involvement" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Shoulder injury" -> "pain and tenderness" -> "internal rotation weakness" -> "supraspinatus muscle involvement" -> 60%
CHAIN: "Shoulder injury" -> "pain and tenderness" -> "internal rotation weakness" -> "deltoid muscle involvement" -> 50%
CHAIN: "Shoulder injury" -> "pain and tenderness" -> "internal rotation weakness" -> "infraspinatus muscle involvement" -> 55%
enhanced_information: The patient's symptoms of weakness in internal rotation against resistance and mild tenderness on palpation are most specific for an injury to the subscapularis muscle, not the infraspinatus muscle as initially suggested. The evidence paths do not provide additional relevant information to support this conclusion.
analysis: The patient's symptoms, particularly the weakness in internal rotation of the arm against resistance, are most specific for an injury to the subscapularis muscle. The subscapularis is part of the rotator cuff and is primarily responsible for internal rotation of the shoulder. The other muscles listed are either involved in different movements or are not the primary muscles for internal rotation.
